seoTitle: How to Integrate Airtable With SharePoint
metaDescription: Connect Airtable to Microsoft SharePoint using a no-code automation platform, since SharePoint isn't a native Airtable Automations action.
intro: Airtable's own Automations panel is useful for triggering actions inside Airtable or pinging apps like Slack, Gmail and Jira, but Microsoft SharePoint isn't one of its native action steps. In practice, "integrate Airtable with SharePoint" means routing the connection through a third-party automation platform such as Make or Zapier. This guide covers what that setup looks like, what triggers and actions are available for this pairing, and where the two accounts need to be connected before anything moves between them.
prerequisites: An Airtable base with the field you'll trigger on (most triggers need a Created Time or Last Modified Time field)
A Microsoft 365 account with write access to the target SharePoint site, list or document library
An account on the automation platform you choose (Make, Zapier or similar)

steps.heading: Confirm Airtable's Automations panel really can't reach SharePoint
steps.body: Airtable's own support documentation lists the native triggers and actions available inside Automations: record-based triggers, scheduled runs, form submissions and webhooks on the trigger side; record updates, emails, Slack messages, and integrations with apps like Google Workspace, Microsoft Outlook, Jira, Salesforce, GitHub and Twilio on the action side. SharePoint doesn't appear anywhere in that list, which is why a native, in-Airtable path to SharePoint doesn't exist.

image.caption: Airtable's template browser. A useful reminder that Airtable's built-in automation options focus on workflows inside Airtable, not external Microsoft services.

steps.heading: Use a connector platform that maintains both integrations
steps.body: Make, Zapier and Integrately all publish dedicated Airtable-to-SharePoint connectors. These platforms sit between the two services: Airtable triggers the workflow, and the platform authenticates with Microsoft and carries out the resulting action in SharePoint. Make's own integration page lists two Airtable triggers, Watch Records and Watch Responses, alongside a long list of SharePoint actions covering folders, files, lists, list items and pages.

image.caption: Make's Airtable-to-SharePoint integration page, showing the Watch Records trigger on the Airtable side and actions like Create a Folder, Create a List, and Create an Item on the SharePoint side.

steps.heading: Pick your Airtable trigger
steps.body: Watch Records, the most common trigger across these platforms, returns newly created or updated records in a view, but it needs a Created Time or Last Modified Time field on your table so the connector can tell what's changed since it last checked. Add one of those fields first if your base doesn't already have it, or the trigger has nothing to key off.

steps.heading: Choose the SharePoint action
steps.body: On the SharePoint side, the available actions run wider than a single create step: creating a folder, creating a list, creating a list item, and (on Make specifically) updating or deleting an existing item, uploading or downloading a file, and listing items in a library. Pick based on what you're keeping in sync: a folder-per-record structure suits document-heavy workflows, a list item suits anything closer to a database row.

image.caption: Integrately's setup screen for the same pairing, listing trigger options like a record being created or updated in Airtable, or a file or folder being created in SharePoint.

steps.heading: Authenticate both accounts and map the fields
steps.body: Connect an Airtable account, typically via a personal access token or OAuth, and a Microsoft account with permission to write to the target SharePoint site, both inside the automation platform, not inside Airtable itself. Grant only the scopes the connector needs, and double-check which site and list or library you're pointing at before saving. Then match each Airtable column to its SharePoint field, text to text, date to date, and pay attention to anything that doesn't translate cleanly, like linked records or multi-select tags, which usually need to be flattened to plain text or a single value first.

steps.heading: Test on one record before trusting it
steps.body: Run the automation against a single test record and check the result directly in SharePoint instead of trusting a green checkmark in the automation platform. A run reporting success and a correctly formatted result in SharePoint aren't always the same thing, especially the first time a field type gets mapped.

troubleshooting.problem: The automation reports success but the SharePoint item looks wrong or empty
troubleshooting.cause: A field type that doesn't map cleanly, most often an Airtable linked record or multi-select, was sent as-is and SharePoint accepted an empty or malformed value instead of rejecting it outright.
troubleshooting.fix: Add a formula or lookup field in Airtable that flattens the problem field to plain text before the automation reads it, then re-test on the same record.

troubleshooting.problem: New items are landing in the wrong SharePoint site or list
troubleshooting.cause: Automation platforms don't stop you from pointing an action at the wrong site or list; it's a straightforward configuration choice.
troubleshooting.fix: Reopen the action step and confirm the exact site URL and list name before rerunning. It's worth relabeling ambiguous list names in SharePoint itself if this keeps happening.

faq.question: Does Airtable have a native SharePoint action in Automations?
faq.answer: No. Airtable's own documentation lists Slack, Gmail, Microsoft Outlook, Jira and several others among its native automation integrations, but Microsoft SharePoint isn't among them, so connecting the two requires a third-party automation platform such as Make, Zapier or Integrately.

faq.question: Do I need a Microsoft 365 account to connect SharePoint?
faq.answer: Yes. You need an active Microsoft account with write access to the target SharePoint site to authenticate the connection inside whichever automation platform you use.

faq.question: Can the automation update existing SharePoint items, not just create new ones?
faq.answer: On Make, yes: its SharePoint actions include updating and deleting existing items alongside creating new folders, lists and list items. Support for updates varies by platform, so check the specific connector's action list before committing to one.

faq.question: Is this integration one-way or two-way?
faq.answer: As set up here, it's one-way, from Airtable to SharePoint, since the automation triggers on Airtable record changes. Syncing changes back from SharePoint into Airtable would need a second, separate automation with its own trigger.

faq.question: Which platform is easiest for a first Airtable-to-SharePoint connection?
faq.answer: Zapier and Make are the most established options, with the largest support communities if something doesn't map the way you expect. Integrately markets itself on one-click templates for common pairings like this one. Try the free tier of whichever one your team already uses elsewhere before committing to a paid plan.

verifiedNote: The claim that Airtable Automations has no native SharePoint action was re-checked against Airtable's own automations documentation in September 2026, and confirmed. The specific trigger and action names for the connector route were checked against Make's own Airtable-SharePoint integration page the same day; the update and delete actions for existing SharePoint items were added to this guide based on that check.
